# What an economic order is {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Three questions describe any order {.scrollable}

An **international order** is a set of rules, institutions and expectations governing relations between states, backed by some distribution of power. The **economic order** is the part that governs trade, money and investment: tariff commitments and their exceptions, exchange-rate and capital-account arrangements, the treatment of foreign investors and their property, and the procedures for settling disputes about all of these.

| Question | Look at |
|---|---|
| **Who wrote the rules?** | Which states designed the institutions, in whose interest |
| **What do the rules say?** | Openness to trade, capital, investment; dispute settlement |
| **What holds them in place?** | Hegemonic power · shared interest · institutional momentum |

Use the three questions as a checklist for any order, past or present: today's session applies them to the post-1945 order; Session 03 asks what happens to the third when power shifts.

The first question is about history, the second about law, the third about politics. A firm's exposure is largely a matter of the third: rules held in place by one state's power are as durable as that power and that state's willingness to use it.

| Answer to the third question | Who | The claim |
|---|---|---|
| **A stabiliser** | Kindleberger (1973) | The interwar collapse happened because no state was both able and willing to stabilise the system — Britain no longer able, the US not yet willing |
| **Hegemonic stability** | Krasner (1976) | Openness is most likely when one state is dominant: it gains most from openness and has the means to enforce it |
| **Institutions** | Keohane (1984), *After Hegemony* | Once built, institutions sustain cooperation after the hegemon declines, because they cut the cost of making and monitoring agreements |

Whether the post-1945 order outlives the relative decline of its authors is the empirical test of that debate — and it is being run now.

::: {.get}
The multinational lives inside the economic order without noticing — until it changes. None of its assumptions — equal tariffs, procedural disputes, convertible dollars, respected patents — is a law of nature.
:::

# The post-1945 order {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four layers {.scrollable}

| Layer | When | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **Bretton Woods** | 1944 | IMF and IBRD; fixed but adjustable rates, dollar anchored on gold |
| **GATT** | 1947 | Tariff-cutting rounds; most-favoured-nation; national treatment |
| **Embedded liberalism** | 1950s–70s | Openness abroad, protection and autonomy at home (Ruggie 1982) |
| **Neoliberal turn and WTO** | 1971–2001 | Gold link ends; capital opens; WTO 1995 with binding disputes, TRIPS, TRIMs; China joins 2001 |

::: {.muted}
Read the layers as a sequence of bargains, not one design. The early order managed openness — capital controls were normal and free trade was managed — so that it stayed politically sustainable at home. The later layers opened capital and reached into services, intellectual property and investment, with rulings that bind.
:::

- **Bretton Woods, July 1944:** forty-four allied nations at the Mount Washington Hotel; Keynes for the UK, Harry Dexter White for the US Treasury. The US held most of the world's monetary gold and was the only major economy undamaged by the war — hence the voting shares, the Washington headquarters, the dollar. *Multilateral in form, American in its foundations.*
- **GATT, 1947:** the planned International Trade Organization was never ratified by the US; the "provisional" GATT survived.
- **15 August 1971:** Nixon suspends dollar–gold convertibility and imposes an import surcharge, without consulting the IMF. Floating by 1973. The rule ended unilaterally; the institutions survived. *The order changed form without collapsing.*
- **WTO, 1995:** born of the Uruguay Round launched in 1986. Rules behind the border (services, TRIPS, TRIMs) and an Appellate Body, so rulings can no longer be blocked by the loser. China joined in 2001 after **fifteen years** of negotiation.

::: {.step}
**Firms as authors, not only subjects.** Sell (2003): a coalition of chief executives from US pharmaceutical, software and entertainment firms framed intellectual property as a *trade* issue in the 1980s; in her account, **twelve corporations** effectively drafted the core of TRIPS. Investment protection came through bilateral treaties instead — the first between West Germany and Pakistan in **1959**, the ICSID Convention in **1965**, a multiplication in the 1990s — letting an investor sue a host state directly.
:::

::: {.muted}
Sources: Eichengreen (2019); Ruggie (1982); Sell (2003).
:::

## Easy to join, hard to overturn {.scrollable}

> The American-led order was open, rule-based and institutional enough that rising states gain more by joining than by challenging it.

::: {.muted}
Ikenberry, G. J. (2011). *Liberal Leviathan*. Princeton UP.
:::

This is the liberal answer to the third question — what holds the rules in place. On this view, institutions have a momentum of their own: a rising power such as China, which joined the WTO in 2001, gains more from the rules than it would from overturning them. The institutions **bind the hegemon too**, which gives others a reason to accept them.

::: {.warn}
The rules a firm relies on are not all of a piece: some multilateral (tariff bindings), some bilateral (investment treaties), some private (standards, Session 06). They will fail in different ways.
:::

::: {.step}
Session 03 sets the realist reply beside it: orders reflect power, and change when power does.
:::

# Baldwin's three unbundlings {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Three costs {.scrollable}

Baldwin organises globalisation around the cost of moving three things. Each time one of them falls, production can be split from something it used to be tied to.

::: {.get}
**Unbundling** — the separation, made possible by a fall in a particular cost of distance, of activities that previously had to take place in the same location: first production from consumption, then the stages of production from one another.
:::

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### Goods

Steam, railways, steamships. Fell from the 19th century: things could be made far from where they were bought — a factory in Manchester could clothe customers in India.

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### Ideas

Telecoms, the internet. Fell from about 1990: a factory abroad could be coordinated from headquarters. For the US, Mexico; for Germany, Poland and central Europe; for Japan, the rest of East Asia.

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

### People

Still expensive. Telepresence and telerobotics may change that, by letting a worker in one country perform services in another without travelling. A forecast, not a finding — the least developed part of the argument.

::::

:::::

::: {.step}
**Regional, not global.** Baldwin & Lopez-Gonzalez (2015): supply-chain trade is organised around three hubs — "Factory North America", "Factory Europe", "Factory Asia" — each pairing high-technology headquarter economies with lower-wage neighbours. The second unbundling was less a globalisation than a set of regionalisations.
:::

::: {.muted}
Baldwin, R. (2016). *The Great Convergence*. Belknap / Harvard UP.
:::

## Divergence, then convergence {.scrollable}

| | Cheap to move | Unbundled | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First unbundling** | goods | production from consumption | Industry clusters in the North → **great divergence** |
| **Second unbundling** | ideas | the factory itself | Know-how moves South **inside value chains** → **great convergence** |
| **Third (prospective)** | people, virtually | worker from workplace | Competition by task and occupation |

In the first unbundling, ideas still moved cheaply only within a region, so industry stayed clustered where it began — Britain, western Europe, North America, later Japan. Comparative advantage was a national property. In the second, stages of production could be offshored while know-how travelled with them, inside firms.

- When a Japanese firm moved assembly to Thailand, it moved the **know-how** too: process engineering, quality systems, managerial practice — under its own control
- **Global value chain:** a production process split into stages in different countries, coordinated by a lead firm, so that what crosses borders is increasingly intermediate goods, services and know-how

::: {.get}
In the second unbundling, **the multinational is the vehicle of convergence**. Technology, jobs and security dependence now travel together — through the supply chain. That is why geopolitics now reaches firms so directly: the export controls of the 2020s on advanced semiconductors and the equipment to make them try to stop exactly the flow the second unbundling made cheap.
:::

## Baldwin's evidence — today's target {.scrollable}

::: {.step}
The **G7 share of world GDP**: rising for a century, then falling sharply from around 1990.
:::

- Almost all of the gain goes to a few economies — Baldwin's **Industrialising Six**: China, Korea, India, Poland, Indonesia, Thailand
- Ask of the figure: **which dollars?** Current, constant, PPP?
- Note also that the **G7 is not in the data**: the World Bank publishes no G7 aggregate, so you build it by summing the seven members

The turning point coincides with the fall in the cost of moving ideas — that is Baldwin's argument in one picture.

The Industrialising Six account for most of the G7's loss:

| Year | I6 share of world GDP, current US$ |
|---|---|
| 1970 | about 6% |
| 1990 | a little over 5% |
| 2010 | about 16% |
| early 2020s | about a quarter |

Within the six, China dominates — and not in a straight line: part of any year-to-year movement is the dollar, which, when it strengthens, shrinks every other economy in dollar terms without anyone producing less.

::: {.step}
**Three decisions shape the figure:** who is in the numerator (the G7 is a political grouping someone turned into a statistic) · the unit of account (the PPP series starts only in 1990) · who is in the denominator.
:::

::: {.muted}
Source: World Bank, WDI, `NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`, October 2026 release; Baldwin (2016).
:::

::: {.muted}
You rebuild it in the practice round — and then rebuild it at PPP.
:::

# From convergence to backlash {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Rodrik's trilemma {.scrollable}

A country can have at most **two** of deep economic integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics. Each row is one way of choosing.

| Keep | Give up | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| integration + sovereignty | democracy | the golden straitjacket |
| integration + democracy | sovereignty | global federalism |
| sovereignty + democracy | **deep integration** | Bretton Woods compromise |

The golden straitjacket means policies dictated by markets; global federalism means rules made above the state; the Bretton Woods compromise means shallow, managed openness.

Read as history: embedded liberalism was the third row; the neoliberal turn and the WTO pushed towards deep integration — Rodrik's *hyperglobalisation* — and for a while the countries concerned accepted the straitjacket.

::: {.get}
Brexit, the tariff wars that began in 2018, industrial policy, export controls, investment screening, "de-risking": choices of sovereignty and democracy over integration.
:::

::: {.step}
**The China shock (Autor, Dorn & Hanson, 2013):** US local labour markets more exposed to Chinese import competition after 2000 suffered larger falls in manufacturing employment and wages, and higher take-up of public transfers — effects that persisted. The losers were geographically concentrated, adjustment was slow, and the compensation the embedded-liberal bargain promised did not reach them. *A bargain that is not honoured stops being a bargain.*
:::

::: {.muted}
Rodrik, D. (2011). *The Globalization Paradox*. W. W. Norton · Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2013), *AER*.
:::

## Slowbalisation {.scrollable}

- World trade in % of GDP climbs from the 1990s to **2008**, then broadly **flattens**
- Retreat — or a change of form, from goods to services and data?
- A measurement trap: the denominator, GDP, has shifted towards services, which are traded less, in exactly the period in question — so the series alone cannot settle the question

A retreat would show up as reshoring and shorter supply chains; a change of form would show up as goods trade stagnating while services and data flows — poorly measured in trade statistics — keep growing. The *extend* step of the practice round lets you see the flattening and judge it.

::: {.step}
When the writers of the rules produce a much smaller share of the world, two questions follow:
**will the rules be rewritten?** (Session 03) · **will the world split into blocs?** (Session 04)
:::

::: {.warn}
**Interdependence as an instrument.** Hirschman (1945), on Nazi Germany's trade with south-eastern Europe: trade that is a large share of a small partner's total makes the threat of interruption a source of influence. Farrell & Newman (2019): the hubs of financial messaging, dollar clearing and cloud platforms sit in a few jurisdictions — interdependence "weaponised".
:::

::: {.muted}
Hirschman (1945) · Farrell & Newman (2019), *International Security*. Developed in Sessions 08, 10, 11.
:::

# What it means for the multinational {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four implications {.scrollable}

| | |
|---|---|
| **Markets are no longer where the rules are written** | Growing revenue in states that did not design the WTO |
| **The supply chain is a geopolitical object** | What the second unbundling moved, export controls now try to stop |
| **Multilateral protection is weaker** | The WTO Appellate Body cannot hear appeals since December 2019 |
| **Measurement is strategy** | Market rates vs PPP: two different boards, two different plants |

::: {.muted}
Each row turns a fact about the order into an item for a firm's risk register. The third is the most concrete: a panel ruling can now be appealed "into the void" and never become binding, so a discriminatory measure by a trading partner is more likely to be settled by bargaining or retaliation between governments than by a legal ruling.
:::

- **Appellate Body, December 2019:** its members' terms expired and the United States blocked replacements. Disputes now go by power rather than procedure — so *the firm's own government's bargaining power* becomes part of its risk profile
- **Jurisdictional reach:** a firm that clears payments in dollars, stores data with a provider in one country, or uses components with another's controlled technology has placed part of its operations under that country's law, wherever it is incorporated. China and the EU are building their own instruments of reach

## Put it to the room {.scrollable}

> You brief a board deciding where to build a plant. The G7 share at market rates and at PPP tell different stories. **Which do you show, and why?**

::: {.fragment}
::: {.check}
It depends on the decision: **market rates** for purchasing power to buy what you export; **PPP** for the real size of local production and markets.
:::

At market rates the G7 still looks large; at PPP it looks much smaller, because many goods and services are cheaper in lower-income economies. A firm that shows its board only one of the two has made a strategic choice without stating it.

- **PPP** values output with the relative prices of a common basket of goods and services rather than market exchange rates — what it would cost in a reference country. Non-traded services are where the gap is largest
- The two measures can disagree on the ranking of economies itself — a point Session 03 returns to with data
- A risk analyst's first duty is to show both and say which question each answers

::: {.muted}
Source: World Bank, WDI, `NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.CD` and `NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`, October 2026 release.
:::
:::

# What the figure does not license {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four limits {.scrollable}

1. A falling share is **relative** — the G7 kept growing in absolute terms; the denominator grew faster. A firm selling into the G7 did not lose customers because the line went down
2. In **current dollars**, part of every move is the exchange rate — a reading in any single year can say as much about currency markets as about convergence
3. Convergence is **concentrated** — above all in China; "the South" did not converge; specific economies that joined specific supply chains did
4. It shows **income**, not **rule-making power**

Each limit is a conclusion a reader might draw from the chart and that the data do not support — the template for today's catch.

::: {.warn}
That last one is a question for Session 03, not a reading of this chart. Hegemonic stability theory predicts that a shrinking share means shrinking rule-making power; institutionalists predict that rules can outlast the share. The chart cannot settle the dispute, because it does not measure the thing in dispute.
:::

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Pivot, then share

DataBank gives you **years as columns**; Tableau wants **one row per country-year**. Pivoting turns the wide table into a long one.

1. Data source pane → select all year columns → right-click → **Pivot**
2. Rename: `Pivot Field Names` → `Year`, `Pivot Field Values` → `Value`
3. `Value` → *Number (decimal)*: DataBank's `..` become nulls
4. Calculated field: G7 GDP ÷ World GDP — filter the members on ISO codes, never on names, which are spelt differently from one source to the next ("Korea, Rep.")
5. Check it with **Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total**

::: {.check}
Over to the practice round: team formation first, then rebuild the G7 share.
:::
